q: Ironwood Office Complex installed R-30 continuous exterior insulation. The energy model shows 12% heating energy reduction. Six months after construction, the facilities manager notices moisture staining on interior walls near window openings. An envelope specialist identifies that window installation details didn't account for the thermal break created by the continuous insulation, causing condensation. What LEED lessons does this illustrate?
options: This is purely a construction defect unrelated to LEED
Continuous insulation needs new window detailing; envelope commissioning would have caught it
Moisture problems are only relevant to the Indoor Environmental Quality category
Continuous insulation should be avoided to prevent these problems
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EA concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: commissioning: a quality-focused process that verifies systems meet the owner’s project requirements; energy model: a simulation used to estimate and compare building energy performance; indoor environmental quality: indoor conditions affecting occupant health, comfort, and well-being
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Continuous insulation needs new window detailing; envelope commissioning would have caught it.
logic: High-performance envelope decisions create new detailing complexities. Adding exterior continuous insulation changes wall assembly thermal dynamics, moving the dew point and requiring careful detailing at window openings to maintain the thermal break. This is exactly what envelope commissioning reviews — illustrating why LEED V5 has elevated envelope commissioning to a required element of Enhanced Commissioning.
core_concept: High-performance envelope decisions create new detailing complexities. Adding exterior continuous insulation changes wall assembly thermal dynamics, moving the dew point and requiring careful detailing at window openings to maintain the thermal break. This is exactly what envelope commissioning reviews — illustrating why LEED V5 has elevated envelope commissioning to a required element of Enhanced Commissioning.
evidence_en: High-performance envelope decisions create new detailing complexities. Adding exterior continuous insulation changes wall assembly thermal dynamics, moving the dew point and requiring careful detailing at window openings to maintain the thermal break. This is exactly what envelope commissioning reviews — illustrating why LEED V5 has elevated envelope commissioning to a required element of Enhanced Commissioning.

q: Seacliff Office Park is about to sign a $1.2M contract for aluminum curtain wall from an overseas manufacturer who says 'we don't provide EPDs or HPDs for standard products.' The project is 3 weeks from final contract deadline. What should the LEED coordinator recommend?

Request a LEED CIR asking for exemption from curtain wall documentation requirements
Sign the contract anyway since the manufacturer will probably provide the documents later
Proceed with the contract — EPDs and HPDs are optional for curtain wall products
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the MR concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: documentation: records used to demonstrate compliance with a LEED requirement; EPD: an Environmental Product Declaration reporting verified life-cycle impacts; HPD: a Health Product Declaration reporting product ingredients and health information
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Negotiate EPD/HPD as contract conditions, or switch to a documented alternative supplier.
logic: Material documentation must be confirmed BEFORE contract signing — after the fact, manufacturers have no obligation to provide documentation post-sale. Aluminum curtain wall at $1.2M (10–12% of typical materials cost) and high embodied carbon makes it a critical credit-driver. The LEED coordinator is correct to require documentation as a contract condition.

q: Redwood Innovation Center uses cross-laminated timber (CLT) for its 8-story structure. A whole-building LCA shows the CLT structure has 35% lower GWP for stages A1–A5 than the concrete alternative, but the energy modeler reports the CLT building uses 4% more energy annually due to reduced thermal mass. How should the team evaluate this trade-off in LEED V5?
options: Operational energy always takes priority over embodied carbon in LEED V5
V5 favors CLT — 35% lower upfront carbon now far outweighs 4% operational increase
The HVAC energy increase disqualifies the CLT structure from LEED recognition
The team should choose concrete since it has better thermal mass
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EA concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: energy model: a simulation used to estimate and compare building energy performance; embodied carbon: greenhouse gas emissions associated with materials and construction; innovation: a strategy with significant benefit not adequately addressed by existing LEED credits
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: V5 favors CLT — 35% lower upfront carbon now far outweighs 4% operational increase.
logic: LEED V5's whole-life carbon framework: a 35% reduction in upfront embodied carbon on a large structure represents 800–1,500 tonnes CO₂e avoided immediately and permanently. The 4% HVAC energy increase adds perhaps 20–40 tonnes CO₂e/year — meaning the embodied benefit takes 25–50+ years to be 'used up.' V5 recognizes that upfront carbon has immediate climate impact.

q: Summit Green Tech Campus achieved LEED Gold with 38% energy improvement over ASHRAE 90.1. The communications team wants to claim 'our building uses 38% less energy than a conventional building.' The sustainability manager corrects them. What is the accurate statement?
options: Only GBCI can authorize specific energy performance claims in marketing materials
The claim is inaccurate because LEED buildings cannot compare to conventional buildings
Say '38% less than the ASHRAE 90.1 modeled baseline' — not 'less than a conventional building'
The claim is completely accurate
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EA concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: baseline: the reference case against which project performance is compared; energy performance: the measured or modeled energy use of a building or system; energy and atmosphere: strategies addressing energy demand, efficiency, refrigerants, and renewable energy
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Say '38% less than the ASHRAE 90.1 modeled baseline' — not 'less than a conventional building'.
logic: Marketing claims must be technically accurate. The 38% improvement is measured against the ASHRAE 90.1 Appendix G modeled baseline — a hypothetical building meeting only code minimums — not against an average existing building (which may use far more energy). Stating '38% better than the ASHRAE 90.1 baseline' is the correct, defensible characterization.

logic: The Surrounding Density and Diverse Uses credit is explicitly about location context — uses in the surrounding neighborhood that make the location walkable. q: Northgate Research Institute discovers mid-construction that 8,000 sf of specified no-added-formaldehyde (NAF) hardwood plywood for millwork was substituted by the subcontractor with standard formaldehyde-containing plywood to save $12,000. Pre-occupancy air quality testing shows elevated formaldehyde at 45 ppb (LEED limit: 16.3 ppb). Three options: (A) Remove and replace all affected millwork ($180,000); (B) Conduct a 30-day flush-out and retest; (C) Apply formaldehyde-blocking sealers to all surfaces. Which approach best serves both LEED compliance and occupant health?
options: Option B alone is sufficient — a flush-out dilutes all construction contaminants
Option B is preferred since LEED allows flush-out as an alternative to material replacement
Option C (sealers) is sufficient and is the industry-standard approach
Option A — remove and replace; flush-out and sealers don't address the source
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the MR concept and solve this best-fit question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: best: a word asking for the strongest or most effective option; materials and resources: strategies addressing life-cycle impacts, product selection, sourcing, and waste; product documentation: verified records supporting environmental and material claims
keywords: Choose the option that addresses the stated LEED intent most directly, not a secondary benefit; decisive option: Option A — remove and replace; flush-out and sealers don't address the source.
logic: Source elimination > source control > dilution is the IAQ hierarchy. For a research facility where occupants spend long hours, formaldehyde will continue off-gassing for years from the substituted plywood. Flush-outs only temporarily dilute; sealers may not fully eliminate emissions. Removal and replacement eliminates the source. The subcontractor's $12K unauthorized substitution creating $180K cleanup is a contractual recovery matter.

The subcontractor's $12K unauthorized substitution creating $180K cleanup is a contractual recovery matter.

For a research facility where occupants spend long hours, formaldehyde will continue off-gassing for years from the substituted plywood. Flush-outs only temporarily dilute; sealers may not fully eliminate emissions. Removal and replacement eliminates the source. q: Magnolia Research Laboratory uses 100% outside air (no recirculation) for all lab spaces due to chemical safety requirements, exhausting all air directly to the exterior. The IEQ consultant claims this automatically earns enhanced IAQ credits. The energy consultant says this hurts the energy credit. Who is correct?
options: Both consultants are completely correct — the system earns full marks in both categories
The IEQ consultant is wrong — 100% outside air is not recognized as an IAQ enhancement
Both partially right — IEQ gains Enhanced IAQ; energy uses lab baselines that absorb the cost
100% outside air has no impact on either IEQ or energy performance credits

logic: Laboratory HVAC design involves genuine IEQ-energy tension. 100% outside air IS protective and can earn Enhanced IAQ credit for exceeding minimum ventilation. It also genuinely increases HVAC energy 40–60%. LEED resolves this tension by using lab-appropriate ASHRAE 90.1 baselines (also high energy use), so the energy credit is measured against an appropriate baseline.

q: The Greentown Logistics Center sustainability manager is told 'warehouses are always in bad locations for transit — LT credits will be difficult.' Is this accurate, and what LT strategies are realistic?
options: LT credits are automatically waived for industrial and logistics facilities
Oversimplified — EV, Reduced Parking, Bicycle, and brownfield credits are achievable
Warehouses earn identical LT credits to office buildings in identical locations
The consultant is correct — warehouses cannot earn any LT credits
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the LT concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: brownfield: previously developed land with actual or perceived contamination; credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; location and transportation: strategies that reduce travel impacts through site selection and mobility options
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Oversimplified — EV, Reduced Parking, Bicycle, and brownfield credits are achievable.

EV infrastructure for employee parking and fleet vehicles, right-sized parking (warehouses often over-park), and bicycle facilities for shift workers are realistic. q: Centurion Law Firm is occupying floors 22–28 of a high-rise building. The base building HVAC provides a fixed 12 CFM/person of outdoor air. 12 CFM/person always meets ASHRAE 62.1 regardless of occupancy density

q: Lakeshore Tower water balance: summer (June–Aug) average rainfall = 1.2 inches/month; roof collection area = 15,000 sf; daily toilet flushing demand = 500 gallons. Is the rainwater cistern likely sufficient for summer months?

q: Bluewater Research Institute has a 200-person open-plan office with mechanical ventilation. An innovative startup proposes installing 400 air-purifying plants (one per 50 sf) as a 'natural air purification system.' The institute should install plants only if they replace the mechanical ventilation system entirely

Plants don't replace mechanical ventilation — but add them for biophilic benefits
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EQ concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: mechanical ventilation: outdoor air supplied by fans and ducted systems; credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; indoor environmental quality: conditions affecting indoor air, thermal comfort, lighting, acoustics, and occupants

logic: The 'plants clean air' claim is based on NASA sealed-chamber research that doesn't translate to real buildings with normal air exchange. q: Cascade Tech Park (300,000 sf, 4 buildings) has a central plant with natural gas boilers. The owner wants to electrify but capital cost is significant. The energy consultant proposes phasing: Year 1 heat pumps for Buildings A and B (50% of campus), Year 3 for Buildings C and D. Phased approaches can be credited — Year 1 conversion plus a documented plan
The whole campus must convert simultaneously or no LEED credit is earned
Gas boilers must be replaced with electric equipment regardless of cost or phase

logic: LEED accommodates phased approaches by crediting what is implemented while recognizing committed plans for future phases. q: The Millbrook Corporate Headquarters is 400m from bus stops for 3 routes: Route 1 (50 weekday trips), Route 2 (30 trips), Route 3 (12 trips). One team member argues only Route 1 should count since routes overlap in coverage. Is this correct?

Routes within the same coverage area cancel each other out in LEED calculations
